final_recommendation: The room converged on a comprehensive trilateral package: 75% RVC with labor-value floor, real-time audits through Mexican labor ministry with trilateral observers, 18-month phase-in, explicit carve-outs for inputs lacking North American supply (semiconductors, rare earths) with year-three review, and phased dairy access—all locked into binding trilateral text. Canada committed under explicit U.S. threat of bilateral-only ratification.
minority_objections: Canada initially resisted bundling dairy with auto rules, insisting supply management was a red line
Uncertainty remained on year-three carve-out review mechanism—auto-renewal vs. renegotiation unresolved at close
key_conflicts: U.S. threatened bilateral ratification if Canada did not commit immediately to full package terms
Dairy access vs. Canadian supply management sovereignty
Hard audit enforcement vs. Canadian concerns about supply-chain disruption
Day-one RVC compliance vs. operational reality of inputs with no North American supply
key_concessions: Canada accepted 75% RVC, labor floor, and real-time audits in exchange for transparent triggers and appeal process
U.S. accepted carve-outs for semiconductors/rare earths with year-three review instead of immediate 75% enforcement
Mexico accepted trilateral observer structure in labor audits, balancing sovereignty with enforcement credibility
Canada accepted phased dairy access in exchange for keeping supply management framework intact
red_lines: Canada: dairy supply management framework itself non-negotiable (phased access acceptable)
U.S. Congress: labor enforcement must have real teeth (30-day violation-to-enforcement window)
Auto industry: carve-outs for impossible inputs must be in binding text, not side memo
Labor unions: no phase-in as cover for delaying actual wage/union compliance
ignored_or_underweighted_risks: Year-three carve-out review mechanism left ambiguous—auto-renewal vs. renegotiation could trigger future supply-chain flight
Dispute settlement (Chapter 19) never surfaced despite being historical Canadian priority
Year-five sunset review mentioned but mechanism details deferred
Compliance cost and supplier reorganization timelines acknowledged but not quantified
downstream_risk_variables: Year-three carve-out review outcome determines whether auto supply chains stay or relocate to Asia
Congressional ratification depends on perceiving one coherent package, not three separate deals
Mexican labor ministry audit capacity and political will to enforce against domestic firms
Canadian domestic political backlash on dairy access concessions
Business investment decisions hinge on sunset/review mechanism clarity
uncertainty_notes: Year-three carve-out review trigger unresolved (auto-renewal vs. renegotiation). Year-five sunset review mechanism mentioned but not detailed. Dispute settlement never discussed. Actual dairy access phase-in schedule not specified. Audit notification windows and appeal process structure acknowledged but not locked into text.

marker_evidence.auto_rules_bottleneck: 75% RVC, labor-value floor, and carve-outs for impossible inputs drove multiple rounds of negotiation and shaped the final package structure—Canada's commitment hinged on resolving these terms
marker_evidence.labor_enforcement_key: Real-time audits through Mexican labor ministry with 30-day enforcement window explicitly tied to Congressional ratification multiple times; labor union stated 'my folks kill this deal in ratification' without real enforcement
marker_evidence.canada_dairy_final_issue: Dairy raised as U.S. demand and Canadian red line, but ultimately resolved via phased access without blocking the deal—acknowledged as sensitive but not deal-breaking
marker_evidence.sunset_to_review_compromise: Year-five review with renewal presumption proposed by Canada and accepted to address investment uncertainty, but mechanism details deferred—raised as concern but not fully resolved
marker_evidence.ratification_risk: Congress explicitly threatened to kill trilateral if Canada didn't commit; dairy access and labor enforcement repeatedly framed as Congressional ratification requirements; shaped multiple concessions
marker_evidence.supply_chain_adjustment: 18-month phase-in and carve-outs discussed as operational necessities to avoid offshore relocation, but compliance costs not quantified—acknowledged but not decisive in shaping terms
marker_evidence.us_mexico_first_pressures_canada: USTR explicitly threatened bilateral ratification without Canada ('we're signing the U.S.-Mexico bilateral without you'); Congress reinforced this leverage; drove Canada's final commitment to full package

node: Node 1 - North American Trade Negotiation Room (after the 27 Aug 2018 U.S.-Mexico preliminary agreement, before the final trilateral USMCA package; information cutoff 2018-08-27)
